report_meta.stock_vs_node_note: IMPORTANT: This report's graph node is 'Amazon Web Services' (AWS) — the cloud/hyperscaler arm that matters to this AI/semiconductor supply chain. But you cannot buy AWS by itself: the publicly traded entity is the WHOLE company, Amazon.com, Inc. (AMZN), of which AWS is one segment (~21% of revenue but the majority of profit). So this report covers all of Amazon.com for the financials/valuation, while emphasizing AWS for the supply-chain story.

report_meta.supply_chain_link: AWS is a DEMAND-ENGINE hub at the TOP of this graph (the hyperscaler tier) — its spending funds much of the rest of the chain. Concretely, AWS: (1) BUYS NVIDIA GPUs in 'substantial quantities' (a customer of reports/NVIDIA.json's hyperscaler tier); (2) BUILDS its own custom silicon — Trainium (AI accelerator), Inferentia (inference), and Graviton (Arm CPU) via Annapurna Labs — which makes AWS a custom-ASIC COMPETITOR to NVIDIA and a customer of custom-silicon/IP and optical-DSP players like Marvell (reports/Marvell.json) and Broadcom; those chips are made by TSMC, use HBM from SK Hynix/Samsung/Micron, and are tested by FormFactor (reports/FormFactor.json); (3) HOSTS the AI labs — it is Anthropic's largest investor and signed a >$100B Anthropic deal, and now offers OpenAI models in Bedrock, with multi-gigawatt training commitments from both (the ai_lab tier feeding reports/NVIDIA.json). AWS's ~$200B FY2026 capex is therefore a primary driver of demand for NVIDIA, Marvell, Broadcom, TSMC, the HBM makers, FormFactor (test), and the optical names (Coherent/Lumentum/AAOI) that wire its data centers. KEY THEME: like the other hyperscalers, AWS both BUYS merchant GPUs and BUILDS its own chips — classic 'co-opetition' with NVIDIA.

beginner_glossary.Amazon Web Services (AWS): Amazon's cloud-computing business — it rents computing power, storage, databases, and AI services to companies, governments, and startups over the internet. AWS is ~21% of Amazon's revenue but the majority of its profit, and it is the part of Amazon that matters most to the AI/semiconductor supply chain.
beginner_glossary.Cloud computing / hyperscaler: Instead of owning their own servers, companies rent computing from giant data-center operators ('hyperscalers') like AWS, Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud. Hyperscalers are the biggest buyers of AI chips.
beginner_glossary.Segment (North America / International /: Amazon reports in three segments: North America (US/Canada retail + ads), International (other countries' retail + ads), and AWS (cloud). Profit is concentrated in AWS and, increasingly, advertising.
beginner_glossary.Capex (capital expenditure): Money spent building data centers, buying chips, servers, networking, power, and (for Amazon) fulfillment/robotics and satellites. Amazon plans ~$200B of capex in 2026, mostly for AWS/AI — a key driver of demand for the whole chip chain.
beginner_glossary.Custom silicon (Trainium / Inferentia /: Chips AWS designs itself (via its Annapurna Labs unit). Trainium = AI training/inference accelerator (competes with NVIDIA GPUs); Inferentia = inference chip; Graviton = Arm-based CPU. Designing its own chips lets AWS cut cost and reduce reliance on NVIDIA.
beginner_glossary.Annapurna Labs: The Amazon chip-design team (acquired 2015) behind Trainium, Inferentia, and Graviton.
beginner_glossary.GPU vs ASIC: A GPU (e.g., NVIDIA) is a flexible, off-the-shelf AI chip. An ASIC (like Trainium) is a custom chip tuned for specific work — often cheaper per unit of performance but less flexible. AWS uses BOTH.
beginner_glossary.Bedrock / SageMaker: AWS's AI platforms. Bedrock lets customers use many AI models (Anthropic's Claude, Meta's Llama, Mistral, and now OpenAI) as a managed service; SageMaker is for building/training models. Bedrock is a major AWS AI growth driver.
beginner_glossary.Agentic AI / agent: AI that doesn't just answer once but reasons, plans, and uses tools to do multi-step work. AWS sells agent tools (Strands, AgentCore, Quro/Qwik) and says agents will drive most AI value — and lots of CPU demand (hence Graviton).
beginner_glossary.Anthropic / OpenAI: Leading AI 'labs' (model makers). Amazon is Anthropic's largest investor and signed a >$100B AWS deal with it; OpenAI's models are now on Bedrock. Both made multi-gigawatt training commitments — huge future AWS revenue.
beginner_glossary.Backlog (RPO): Contracted future revenue not yet recognized ('remaining performance obligations'). AWS's backlog was $364B in Q1 2026 — a measure of demand visibility (and that figure excludes the recent >$100B Anthropic deal).
beginner_glossary.Annualized run rate: A quarter's revenue multiplied to a yearly pace. AWS is at a ~$150B annualized run rate; AWS's custom-chip business is at a >$20B run rate (>$50B if it sold all its chips externally).
beginner_glossary.Operating income vs net income: Operating income = profit from running the business (the cleanest operational gauge). Net income = the bottom line after interest, taxes, and gains/losses on investments (Amazon's net income swings with the value of stakes like Anthropic and Rivian).
beginner_glossary.Operating margin: Operating income ÷ revenue. Amazon hit a record 13.1% companywide; AWS alone runs ~37.7% — which is why AWS drives most of the profit.
beginner_glossary.Advertising: Amazon sells ads (sponsored products, Prime Video ads, etc.) — a fast-growing, high-margin business that cleared a >$70B trailing run rate.
beginner_glossary.Prime: Amazon's paid membership (fast shipping, Prime Video, etc.) that drives loyalty and spending.
beginner_glossary.Free cash flow (FCF) / ROIC: FCF = cash left after capex. ROIC = return on invested capital. Amazon's FCF is being SQUEEZED right now because AI capex is growing faster than revenue; management argues the long-run ROIC is attractive once the new capacity is monetized.
beginner_glossary.Memory / HBM cost: Memory chips (DRAM/HBM) have spiked in price due to AI demand. Amazon flagged this as a cost/capex pressure — and it links AWS to memory makers (SK Hynix/Samsung/Micron).
beginner_glossary.Amazon LEO: Amazon's low-earth-orbit satellite network (formerly 'Project Kuiper') for broadband — capital-intensive, launching commercially in 2026; a newer, separate growth bet.
beginner_glossary.P/E and P/S: P/E = price ÷ earnings per share; P/S = market value ÷ revenue. Amazon trades ~28x earnings and ~3.5x sales — far more grounded than the small-cap AI names, because its profits are large and real.

company_snapshot.what_it_is: Amazon.com, Inc. is one of the world's largest companies, spanning three big businesses: (1) AWS — the leading cloud-computing platform and the company's profit engine and AI growth driver; (2) e-commerce/retail — the giant online (and grocery) store, third-party marketplace, and Prime; and (3) advertising — a fast-growing, high-margin business. For THIS supply-chain graph, the relevant node is AWS, the hyperscaler that buys and builds AI chips and hosts AI labs.
company_snapshot.ceo: Andrew R. (Andy) Jassy (President & CEO); Brian T. Olsavsky (CFO)
company_snapshot.founded: 1994 (by Jeff Bezos, who is now Executive Chairman)
company_snapshot.where_it_sits_in_the_chain: Hyperscaler tier (AWS) — a top-of-graph demand engine. AWS buys NVIDIA GPUs, builds its own Trainium/Graviton silicon, and hosts AI labs (Anthropic, OpenAI). Its capex funds much of the chip/optical/test chain below it.
the_three_segments: AWS — cloud computing (~21% of revenue, the majority of operating profit; ~37.7% operating margin)
North America — US/Canada retail, marketplace, ads, devices (~57% of revenue)
International — non-US retail, marketplace, ads (~22% of revenue)
company_snapshot.custom_silicon_note: Via Annapurna Labs, AWS designs Trainium (AI accelerator), Inferentia (inference), and Graviton (Arm CPU). Management says this is now 'one of the top three data center chip businesses in the world,' with >$20B run-rate (>$50B if sold fully externally). It still buys substantial NVIDIA GPUs in parallel.

business_model.summary: Amazon makes money three ways: renting cloud computing (AWS), selling/【facilitating retail (its own goods + a huge third-party marketplace + Prime + grocery), and selling advertising. Retail drives enormous revenue at thin margins; AWS and advertising drive most of the profit. The current story is AWS reaccelerating on AI demand while Amazon pours ~$200B of capex into AI infrastructure (including its own chips) — pressuring near-term free cash flow but, management argues, building very large future revenue and returns.
how_they_make_money: AWS (cloud): renting compute, storage, databases, networking, and AI services (Bedrock, SageMaker). $37.6B in Q1 2026 (+28% YoY) at a ~37.7% operating margin — the profit engine.
North America retail: 1P (own inventory) + 3P marketplace fees + Prime subscriptions + grocery (now the #2 US grocer) + devices. $104.1B in Q1 2026 (+12%).
International retail: the same model outside the US. $39.8B in Q1 2026 (+11% ex-FX).
Advertising: sponsored products, Prime Video ads, etc. $17.2B in Q1 2026 (+22%); a high-margin, >$70B trailing business.

Custom silicon: Trainium/Inferentia/Graviton cut AWS's own costs (expected to save 'tens of billions of capex per year') and are increasingly sold to external customers (Anthropic, OpenAI, Meta, Uber).
competitive_moat_analyst_view: AWS scale + breadth: the broadest, most-adopted cloud, with deep security/operational track record — customers keep their AI inference near their data, which lives in AWS. [Q1 2026 call]
Full chip stack (Trainium + Graviton): owning both the leading price-performance AI accelerator and the leading Arm CPU is a structural cost and margin advantage few rivals match. [Q1 2026 call]
AI-lab anchor tenants: Anthropic (largest investor; >$100B deal) and OpenAI (models on Bedrock) anchor demand and validate Trainium. [Q1 2026 call]
Retail flywheel + Prime + logistics: scale, selection, fast delivery, and a >$70B ads business create a hard-to-replicate consumer moat. [Q1 2026 call]
Capital + know-how to fund ~$200B/year of AI infrastructure — a barrier only a few companies can clear. [Q1 2026 call]

revenue_streams.analyst_view: Amazon is a retail giant with two profit engines (AWS and advertising). AWS is ~21% of revenue but the majority of operating income and essentially all of the AI story; advertising (~9%) is the fast-growing, high-margin sweetener; retail (~79% of revenue) provides scale and cash but thin margins. For this graph, AWS is what matters — and its 28% reacceleration plus the $364B backlog and Trainium commitments are the key signals. The companywide record 13.1% operating margin shows the mix is shifting toward the profitable businesses.

competitors.landscape_summary: Amazon competes on multiple fronts. In cloud, AWS competes with Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud (and Oracle, CoreWeave). In custom AI silicon, AWS's Trainium competes with NVIDIA GPUs (and with Google's TPU and Microsoft's Maia) while relying on partners like Marvell/Broadcom and TSMC to build chips. In retail, it competes with Walmart and others; in advertising, with Google and Meta.

competitors.supply_chain_cross_reference: AWS's GPU supplier/competitor NVIDIA, its custom-silicon partners Marvell/Broadcom, foundry TSMC, memory makers (SK Hynix/Samsung/Micron), test supplier FormFactor, and AI-lab tenants Anthropic/OpenAI are all nodes in this repo. AWS sits ATOP this stack: its ~$200B capex is a primary demand source for all of them.
competitors.differentiation_analyst_view: AWS differentiates on breadth, scale, security/track record, and a unique two-chip stack (Trainium + Graviton) that lowers cost. Its main competitive risks are Azure and Google Cloud (both strong in AI and also building custom silicon) and the broader question of whether hyperscaler capex earns its return. Amazon's 'co-opetition' with NVIDIA — buying GPUs while building Trainium — mirrors the rest of the hyperscaler field.

financial_performance.analyst_view: Operationally Amazon is firing well: record 13.1% operating margin, AWS reaccelerating to 28% at a ~38% margin, advertising +22%, and retail efficiency improving. The big debate is the ~$200B capex: it is depressing free cash flow now (a real near-term negative), and the bull case rests on that AI/AWS capacity earning strong returns — which management argues (and the $364B+ backlog and Trainium commitments support) but which won't be proven until the spend is monetized. Use operating income/segment margins and the backlog to judge the business; net income is noisier due to investment marks.

implied_multiples_analyst_view.interpretation: Unlike the small-cap AI names in this repo (often 20–65x sales), Amazon trades at ~28x earnings and ~3.5x sales — a reasonable multiple for a mega-cap growing mid-teens with a reaccelerating, ~38%-margin AWS engine and a high-margin ads business. The key valuation nuance is FREE CASH FLOW: today's ~$200B capex compresses FCF, so the stock is valued on the EXPECTATION that AI/AWS investments will convert to large future cash flows. A 'sum-of-the-parts' lens (AWS as a high-margin grower, ads as a high-margin grower, retail as a scale/cash business) is how many analysts justify upside.
implied_multiples_analyst_view.what_would_change_it: Durability of AWS growth and margins, the ROI on $200B of capex, advertising's trajectory, and retail efficiency are the swing factors.

valuation.analyst_view: Amazon is the most reasonably valued, most diversified, and most cash-generative name in this cluster — a mega-cap with multiple profit engines rather than a single-thesis AI bet. The honest tension is the capex/FCF squeeze: the market is paying ~28x earnings on the belief that ~$200B/year of AI investment earns strong returns. If AWS growth and capex ROI hold, the analyst consensus (~$313, ~30% above the price) looks reasonable; if AI capex disappoints or AWS decelerates, the FCF drag becomes the story.

risks.why_it_matters: ~$200B FY2026 capex is growing faster than revenue, compressing free cash flow now; the payoff depends on monetizing the new capacity at good returns.
If AWS growth slows or AI workloads underdeliver economically, the huge capex earns weak returns — the central bear case for all hyperscalers.
Strong rivals are also reaccelerating and building custom silicon; share/pricing pressure could cap AWS growth and margins.
Spiking DRAM/HBM prices raise data-center costs and capex; supply constraints could limit capacity additions.
Trainium must keep its price-performance edge and ramp (3→4) on time; mismanaging the NVIDIA relationship or chip roadmap would hurt.
Recession, tariffs, or weak consumer spending hit the large (thin-margin) retail business and international results.
Amazon faces antitrust and regulatory scrutiny (marketplace practices, cloud, M&A like Globalstar) across the US, EU, and elsewhere.
Satellites and robotaxis are capital-heavy and early; they add cost (~$1B/yr LEO step-up) before meaningful returns.
Equity stakes (Anthropic, Rivian) swing GAAP net income, making the bottom line noisy quarter to quarter.

final_research_summary.one_paragraph: Amazon.com, Inc. (AMZN; graph node 'Amazon Web Services') is a ~$2.6T mega-cap with three businesses — AWS (cloud), retail/marketplace, and advertising — but for this AI/semiconductor supply chain the relevant node is AWS, the hyperscaler that buys NVIDIA GPUs, builds its own Trainium/Graviton chips, and hosts the AI labs (Anthropic, OpenAI). The quarter was strong: Q1 2026 (reported 2026-04-29) revenue was $181.5B (+17% YoY) with a RECORD 13.1% operating margin ($23.9B operating income), and the standout was AWS reaccelerating to $37.6B (+28% YoY, a 15-quarter high) at a ~37.7% margin and a ~$150B run rate, with a $364B backlog that EXCLUDES a recent >$100B Anthropic deal. AWS's custom-silicon business is now a 'top-3 data-center chip business' (>$20B run rate, >$50B if sold fully externally) with >$225B of Trainium commitments, even as Amazon keeps buying substantial NVIDIA GPUs — classic hyperscaler 'co-opetition.' The central tension is capital: Amazon plans ~$200B of capex in FY2026 (mostly AWS/AI), which is growing faster than revenue and CONSTRAINING free cash flow now; management argues (and the backlog/commitments support) that this builds very large future revenue and attractive multi-year ROIC, but that won't be proven until the capacity is monetized. On valuation, Amazon is far more grounded than the small-cap AI names — ~28x trailing earnings and ~3.5x sales — and analysts are strongly bullish (Strong Buy; ~$313 average target, ~30% above the ~$239 price). The facts (record margins, AWS reacceleration, $364B+ backlog, Trainium scale, ads >$70B) are strong and well-documented; what is debated is the RETURN on ~$200B/year of AI capex and the durability of AWS growth against Azure/Google Cloud. The core debate is capex-ROI + AWS durability, not whether Amazon is a quality, cash-generative franchise.
